name: Pectoralis Major
origin: Clavicular head: Anterior surface of medial half of clavicle
Sternocostal head: Anterior surface of sternum, superior six costal cartilages, aponeurosis of external oblique
insertion: Lateral lip of bicipital groove (intertubercular sulcus) of humerus
innervation: Lateral and medial pectoral nerves (Clavicular head: C5, C6; Sternocostal head: C7, C8, T1)
arterialSupply: Pectoral branch of thoracoacromial trunk, internal thoracic artery
primaryActions: Adduction and medial rotation of humerus at glenohumeral joint
Clavicular head: Flexes humerus
Sternocostal head: Extends humerus from flexed position
clinicalRelevance: Can be harvested for reconstructive surgery (breast reconstruction or facial reanimation). Absence or hypoplasia is a hallmark of Poland syndrome. Used to test spinal levels C5 to T1 during clinical manual muscle testing.

name: Deltoid
origin: Anterior part: Lateral third of clavicle
Middle part: Acromion process of scapula
Posterior part: Spine of scapula
insertion: Deltoid tuberosity of humerus
arterialSupply: Posterior circumflex humeral artery, deltoid branch of thoracoacromial artery
primaryActions: Middle part: Principal abductor of humerus (from 15 to 90 degrees)
Anterior part: Flexion and medial rotation of humerus
Posterior part: Extension and lateral rotation of humerus
clinicalRelevance: Common site for intramuscular drug injections. The axillary nerve is highly vulnerable during anterior shoulder dislocation or surgical neck of humerus fractures, leading to deltoid paralysis, atrophy, and loss of arm abduction.

name: Biceps Brachii
origin: Short head: Apex of coracoid process of scapula
Long head: Supraglenoid tubercle of scapula
insertion: Radial tuberosity and bicipital aponeurosis into deep fascia of forearm
primaryActions: Powerful supinator of forearm (when elbow is flexed)
Flexor of forearm at elbow joint
Weak accessory flexor of arm at glenohumeral joint
clinicalRelevance: Tested clinically using the biceps reflex (C5-C6). Rupture of the long head tendon leads to a distinct bulge in the lower arm known as the 'Popeye deformity'.

name: Triceps Brachii
origin: Long head: Infraglenoid tubercle of scapula
Lateral head: Posterior surface of humerus, superior to radial groove
Medial head: Posterior surface of humerus, inferior to radial groove
insertion: Olecranon process of ulna
primaryActions: Primary extensor of forearm at elbow joint
Long head: Resists downward displacement of humeral head during abduction
clinicalRelevance: Tested clinically via the triceps reflex (C7-C8). Fractures of the olecranon disrupt the extensor mechanism. Radial nerve damage in the axilla (crutch palsy) paralyzes all three heads, while damage in the radial groove usually spares the long head.

name: Brachioradialis
origin: Proximal two-thirds of lateral supracondylar ridge of humerus
insertion: Lateral surface of distal end of radius, proximal to styloid process
primaryActions: Flexion of forearm at elbow joint when forearm is in mid-prone position
clinicalRelevance: The only muscle supplied by the radial nerve that acts as a flexor. Evaluated clinically during the supinator/brachioradialis reflex (C5-C6). Landmark for finding the radial artery in the wrist.

name: Pronator Teres
origin: Humeral head: Medial epicondyle of humerus (common flexor origin)
Ulnar head: Coronoid process of ulna
insertion: Middle of lateral surface of shaft of radius
arterialSupply: Ulnar artery, anterior ulnar recurrent artery
primaryActions: Pronation of forearm
Weak flexor of elbow joint
clinicalRelevance: Hypertrophy or repetitive overuse can entrap the median nerve between the humeral and ulnar heads, a clinical condition known as Pronator Teres Syndrome (presenting with paresthesia in the lateral 3.5 digits).

name: Flexor Carpi Radialis
origin: Medial epicondyle of humerus (common flexor origin)
insertion: Base of second metacarpal bone (with a slip to the third)
primaryActions: Flexion of hand at wrist joint
Abduction (radial deviation) of hand at wrist joint
clinicalRelevance: Its tendon serves as an essential landmark for finding and palpating the radial pulse. It passes through a separate compartment of the flexor retinaculum, which can be affected in localized tenosynovitis.

name: Extensor Digitorum
origin: Lateral epicondyle of humerus (common extensor origin)
insertion: Extensor expansions of medial four digits
innervation: Posterior interosseous nerve (C7, C8; branch of radial nerve)
arterialSupply: Posterior interosseous artery, recurrent interosseous artery
primaryActions: Extends medial four digits at metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints
Assists in hand extension (wrist dorsiflexion)
clinicalRelevance: Overuse of this muscle and other extensors causes common extensor tendinopathy, popularly known as 'Tennis Elbow' (lateral epicondylitis). Injury to the terminal tendon at the DIP joint results in Mallet Finger.

name: Opponens Pollicis
origin: Flexor retinaculum and tubercle of trapezium bone
insertion: Entire length of lateral border of first metacarpal bone
innervation: Recurrent branch of median nerve (C8, T1)
arterialSupply: Superficial palmar branch of radial artery
primaryActions: Opposes the thumb (flexes, abducts, and medially rotates the first metacarpal at the carpometacarpal joint)
clinicalRelevance: Opposition is the most crucial hand movement for human grip. Atrophy of thenar muscles occurs in severe Carpal Tunnel Syndrome, leading to 'Ape Hand deformity' where thumb opposition is lost.

name: Gluteus Maximus
origin: Outer surface of ilium posterior to posterior gluteal line
Dorsal surface of sacrum and coccyx
Sacrotuberous ligament
insertion: Most fibers insert into the iliotibial tract; deeper fibers insert into the gluteal tuberosity of femur
arterialSupply: Superior and inferior gluteal arteries, first perforating branch of profunda femoris
primaryActions: Powerful extensor of thigh at hip joint (essential for climbing stairs, standing up from sitting)
Lateral rotator of thigh
Steadies thigh and assists in locking knee joint via iliotibial tract
clinicalRelevance: Evaluated during gait analysis; weakness leads to 'Gluteus Maximus Lurch' (the trunk is thrown backward during the stance phase to prevent flexion of the hip). Site for deep gluteal IM injections (upper outer quadrant to avoid sciatic nerve).

name: Gluteus Medius
origin: Outer surface of ilium between anterior and posterior gluteal lines
insertion: Lateral surface of greater trochanter of femur
primaryActions: Abducts thigh at hip joint
Medially rotates thigh (anterior fibers)
Steadies pelvis during single-leg stance, preventing the contralateral side of the pelvis from dropping
clinicalRelevance: Injury to the superior gluteal nerve or gluteus medius results in a positive Trendelenburg test. When the patient stands on the affected leg, the pelvis drops on the opposite (unsupported) side, leading to a Trendelenburg gait ('waddling' gait).

name: Rectus Femoris
origin: Straight head: Anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS)
Reflected head: Groove superior to acetabulum
insertion: Base of patella and, via the patellar ligament, into tibial tuberosity
primaryActions: Extends leg at knee joint
Flexes thigh at hip joint (the only quadriceps muscle that crosses both joints)
clinicalRelevance: Tested clinically during the patellar reflex (Knee Jerk, L3-L4). Prone to rectus femoris strains ('kicking injury') in athletes. AIIS avulsion fractures can occur in adolescent athletes.

name: Biceps Femoris
origin: Long head: Ischial tuberosity (common hamstring origin)
Short head: Linea aspera and lateral supracondylar ridge of femur
insertion: Lateral side of head of fibula
innervation: Long head: Tibial division of sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2); Short head: Common fibular division of sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2)
arterialSupply: Perforating branches of profunda femoris, inferior gluteal artery, superior lateral genicular artery
primaryActions: Flexes leg at knee joint and laterally rotates tibia when knee is flexed
Extends thigh at hip joint (long head only)
clinicalRelevance: Hamstring strains are highly common in running or sprinting athletes. Its tendon forms the superolateral boundary of the popliteal fossa, where the common fibular nerve runs close to its medial border.

name: Semitendinosus
origin: Ischial tuberosity
insertion: Superior medial shaft of tibia (as part of Pes Anserinus)
innervation: Tibial division of sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2)
arterialSupply: Perforating branches of profunda femoris, inferior gluteal artery
primaryActions: Flexes leg at knee joint and medially rotates tibia when knee is flexed
Extends thigh at hip joint
clinicalRelevance: The tendon of semitendinosus is frequently harvested for ACL reconstructive surgery. It is a member of the 'Pes Anserinus' group (Sartorius, Gracilis, Semitendinosus), which can be involved in Pes Anserine bursitis.

name: Gastrocnemius
origin: Lateral head: Lateral aspect of lateral condyle of femur
Medial head: Popliteal surface of femur, superior to medial condyle
insertion: Posterior surface of calcaneus via the Achilles (calcaneal) tendon
primaryActions: Plantarflexion of foot at ankle joint
Flexion of leg at knee joint
clinicalRelevance: Rupture of the calcaneal tendon is highly disabling; diagnosed with the Thompson (Simmonds) squeeze test. Rupture of medial head during sudden eccentric extension of knee results in 'Tennis Leg'.

name: Soleus
origin: Posterior aspect of head and superior shaft of fibula
Soleal line and medial border of tibia
insertion: Posterior surface of calcaneus via the Achilles (calcaneal) tendon
arterialSupply: Posterior tibial, peroneal, and popliteal arteries
primaryActions: Plantarflexion of foot at ankle joint (independent of knee position)
clinicalRelevance: Known as the 'peripheral heart' because its strong contraction during gait pushes venous blood superiorly through deep veins. Important in postural stability during standing.

name: Tibialis Anterior
origin: Lateral condyle and superior half of lateral surface of tibia, interosseous membrane
insertion: Medial and inferior surfaces of medial cuneiform and base of first metatarsal
primaryActions: Dorsiflexion of foot at ankle joint
Inversion of foot at subtalar joints
clinicalRelevance: Injury to deep fibular nerve leads to complete loss of dorsiflexion, causing Foot Drop. Overuse of tibialis anterior is a leading cause of anterior tibial stress syndrome, or 'shin splints'.

name: Frontalis (part of Occipitofrontalis)
origin: Epicranial aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica)
insertion: Skin and subcutaneous tissue of eyebrows and forehead
innervation: Temporal branch of facial nerve (CN VII)
arterialSupply: Ophthalmic, superficial temporal, and posterior auricular arteries
primaryActions: Raises eyebrows
Wrinkles skin of forehead horizontally (expressing surprise or worry)
clinicalRelevance: Paralyzed in facial nerve lesions (Bell's Palsy). In upper motor neuron (UMN) lesions, the forehead is spared due to bilateral cortical representation, whereas in lower motor neuron (LMN) lesions, the forehead is fully paralyzed on the affected side.

name: Orbicularis Oculi
origin: Medial palpebral ligament, nasal part of frontal bone, lacrimal bone
insertion: Skin around margin of orbit, tarsal plate
innervation: Temporal and zygomatic branches of facial nerve (CN VII)
arterialSupply: Facial, superficial temporal, and ophthalmic arteries
primaryActions: Palpebral part: Closes eyelids gently (blinking)
Orbital part: Closes eyelids tightly (squinting, protecting eye)
clinicalRelevance: Weakness prevents complete eye closure (lagophthalmos), leading to corneal drying, ulceration, and ectropion (eversion of lower eyelid), commonly observed in patients with Bell's Palsy.

name: Masseter
origin: Maxillary process of zygomatic bone, lower border of zygomatic arch
insertion: Lateral surface of ramus and angle of mandible
innervation: Masseteric nerve (branch of mandibular division of trigeminal nerve CN V3)
primaryActions: Elevates mandible (closes jaw forcefully during chewing)
Assists in protraction of mandible
clinicalRelevance: The strongest muscle of mastication. Tetanus (lockjaw) specifically targets the masseter, causing painful tonic spasms. Hypertrophy of the masseter is associated with bruxism (teeth grinding) and TMJ dysfunction.

name: Sternocleidomastoid
origin: Sternal head: Anterior surface of manubrium of sternum
Clavicular head: Superior surface of medial third of clavicle
insertion: Lateral surface of mastoid process of temporal bone, lateral half of superior nuchal line
innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI, motor); C2, C3 spinal nerves (pain and proprioception)
primaryActions: Unilateral: Flexes neck laterally, rotates head to face opposite side
Bilateral: Flexes neck forward, raises chin
clinicalRelevance: Spasmodic contraction or shortening of this muscle causes Congenital Torticollis (wryneck), causing the head to tilt toward the affected side and rotation of the face to the opposite side. Landmark separating anterior and posterior triangles of neck.

name: Trapezius
origin: Medial third of superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance, ligamentum nuchae
Spinous processes of C7 to T12 vertebrae
insertion: Lateral third of clavicle, acromion process, and spine of scapula
innervation: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI, motor); C3, C4 spinal nerves (proprioception)
primaryActions: Upper fibers: Elevate scapula
Middle fibers: Retract (adduct) scapula
Lower fibers: Depress scapula
Together: Rotate scapula superiorly during abduction of arm
clinicalRelevance: Tested by shrugging the shoulders against resistance (CN XI test). Weakness causes shoulder drooping and dynamic scapular winging during arm abduction (inability to raise arm above horizontal plane).

name: Latissimus Dorsi
origin: Spinous processes of T7 to T12 vertebrae
Thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest
Inferior 3 or 4 ribs
insertion: Floor of intertubercular (bicipital) groove of humerus
primaryActions: Extends, adducts, and medially rotates humerus at glenohumeral joint (known as the 'climbing' or 'swimming' muscle)
Depresses scapula
clinicalRelevance: Surgical flaps of latissimus dorsi are widely used for autologous breast reconstruction. Vital for wheelchair propulsion and using crutches. Injury to the thoracodorsal nerve during axillary node dissections impairs arm extension.

name: Erector Spinae
origin: Broad tendon from posterior part of iliac crest, posterior surface of sacrum, sacroiliac ligaments
Sacral and inferior lumbar spinous processes
insertion: Spinalis: Spinous processes of upper thoracic and cervical vertebrae
Longissimus: Ribs between angles and tubercles, transverse processes of thoracic and cervical vertebrae, mastoid process
Iliocostalis: Angles of lower ribs, transverse processes of cervical vertebrae
innervation: Posterior rami of spinal nerves of respective regions
arterialSupply: Lateral sacral, lumbar, intercostal, and occipital arteries
primaryActions: Bilateral: Extends vertebral column and head (vital for maintaining erect posture)
Unilateral: Flexes vertebral column laterally
clinicalRelevance: The primary postural stabilizer. Repetitive strain or lifting with a flexed spine can cause acute erector spinae spasms, leading to lower back pain. Target of postural retraining and core stabilization exercises in physiotherapy.

name: Pectoralis Minor
origin: Anterior surfaces of 3rd, 4th, and 5th ribs near their costal cartilages
insertion: Coracoid process of scapula (medial border and superior surface)
primaryActions: Stabilizes scapula by drawing it inferiorly and anteriorly against thoracic wall
Auxiliary muscle of respiration (elevates ribs when scapula is fixed)
clinicalRelevance: Can contract pathologically, resulting in Pectoralis Minor Syndrome (characterized by compression of the brachial plexus and axillary vessels under the coracoid process, a type of Thoracic Outlet Syndrome). Key surgical landmark in the axilla.

name: Serratus Anterior
origin: External surfaces of lateral parts of 1st to 8th ribs
insertion: Anterior (costal) surface of medial border of scapula
innervation: Long thoracic nerve (of Bell) (C5, C6, C7)
primaryActions: Protracts scapula and holds it firmly against thoracic wall (called the 'boxer's muscle')
Rotates scapula upward to allow abduction of arm past 90 degrees
clinicalRelevance: Injury to the long thoracic nerve (e.g., during axillary clearance or chest tube insertion) paralyzes this muscle, causing 'Winging of Scapula'. The medial border of the scapula lifts off the thoracic wall, especially when pushing against a wall.

name: Diaphragm
origin: Sternal part: Posterior aspect of xiphoid process
Costal part: Internal surfaces of lower 6 ribs and costal cartilages
Lumbar part: L1-L3 vertebral bodies (via medial/lateral arcuate ligaments and right/left crura)
insertion: Central tendon of diaphragm
innervation: Phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5 - 'keep the diaphragm alive')
arterialSupply: Pericardiacophrenic, musculophrenic, and superior/inferior phrenic arteries
primaryActions: The primary muscle of respiration (descends during inspiration, increasing thoracic volume and drawing air in)
clinicalRelevance: Phrenic nerve injury paralyzes a hemi-diaphragm, presenting as paradoxical breathing. Congenital or acquired defects can lead to diaphragmatic hernias (e.g., Bochdalek hernia), allowing abdominal viscera into the chest.

name: Rectus Abdominis
origin: Pubic crest and pubic symphysis
insertion: Xiphoid process of sternum and 5th to 7th costal cartilages
innervation: Thoracoabdominal nerves (anterior rami of T7 to T12 spinal nerves)
primaryActions: Flexes trunk (vertebral column)
Compresses abdominal viscera (increases intra-abdominal pressure during defecation, micturition, parturition, and forced expiration)
clinicalRelevance: Separated along the midline by the linea alba, which can separate during pregnancy, a condition called 'diastasis recti'. Highly active in spinal stabilization and posture. Incision site for laparotomies.

name: External Oblique
origin: External surfaces of 5th to 12th ribs
insertion: Linea alba, pubic tubercle, anterior half of iliac crest
arterialSupply: Deep circumflex iliac and superficial circumflex iliac arteries, lower intercostal arteries
primaryActions: Compresses abdominal viscera and supports trunk
Bilateral: Flexes trunk forward
Unilateral: Flexes trunk laterally and rotates trunk to the opposite side
clinicalRelevance: The lower free border of the external oblique aponeurosis folds under to form the inguinal ligament (Poupart's ligament), which is a key anatomical landmark for the inguinal canal and repair of inguinal hernias.

name: Sartorius
origin: Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)
insertion: Superior part of medial surface of tibia (as part of Pes Anserinus)
primaryActions: Flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates thigh at hip joint
Flexes and medially rotates leg at knee joint (enables the cross-legged tailor position)
clinicalRelevance: The longest muscle in the human body. Forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle. Can be used as an autologous muscular flap in pelvic reconstruction.
